title: 'Two Out Of Three Ain't Bad' In Movahed's Freestyle Friday Victory
summary: GM Sina Movahed won Freestyle Friday for the second time in three weeks (channeling the old Meat Loaf song) on October 30, despite starting on 1.5/3 points. GM Nodirbek Yakubboev led much of the way, but settled for second place after his 10th-round loss to Movahed as part of the victor's eight-game winning streak. GM Faustino Oro finished third on tiebreaks ahead of fourth-place GM Nguyen Ngoc Truong Son. Movahed, Yakubboev, and Oro all currently hold a qualifying position in the standings for the Freestyle Friday Championship (FFC), which runs through December 4. WFM Anna Cramling played and streamed for Freestyle Chess, which you can view below: Only Oro and GM Zhamsaran Tsydypov made it into the first break unblemished on 4/4. Out of the break, Oro missed an early chance to win a piece and later got into time trouble, which ended up costing him four pawns as Tsydypov became the last perfect player. Unfortunately for him, Tsydypov then only scored a combined half-point in his next four rounds and finished 11th.

title: Sarana Wins Early, Arjun Wins Twice In 3 0 Thursday
summary: GM Alexey Sarana won the first 3 0 Thursday with a dominant 10/11 score. Not to be outdone, GM Arjun Erigaisi proceeded to win both the second and third tournaments. It was the second time this year that Arjun won two 3 0 Thursdays on the same day. He joins GM Jose Martinez as just the second player to accomplish the double victory for a second time. Sarana made the first tournament of the day look easy. He won his first six games, including a back-and-forth battle with GM Rudik Makarian in the fifth round.

title: FIDE World U7-U17 Rapid and Blitz Championships 2026 Egypt: Registration deadline extended
summary: The International Chess Federation (FIDE) and the Egyptian Chess Federation are pleased to announce that the registration deadline for the 2026 FIDE World U7–U17 Rapid and Blitz Championships has been extended to 10 November 2026. The event will take place in Cairo, Egypt, from 8 December (arrival) to 15 December (departure) 2026. The participants will compete across six age categories: Under 7, Under 9, Under 11, Under 13, Under 15, and Under 17, with separate Open and Girls sections. Players who secured first place in the previous edition of the FIDE World Rapid & Blitz Cadets & Youth Championships (U9–U17 age groups) are granted the personal right to participate in the corresponding (or higher) age category, provided they meet the age requirement as of January 1, 2026. FIDE Member Federations may register any number of players and accompanying officials/persons. The registration deadline is November 10, 2026. Invitation, regulations, schedule (PDF) Registration details: Registration form: https://forms.gle/sJW3H1QfS5FZ3kqE8 Email: youthrapidblitz@fide.com  Official website: https://youthrapidblitz2026.fide.com

title: FIDE introduces the first members of its administrative team
summary: After announcing its new organisational structure on 26 October 2026, FIDE has begun assembling the team responsible for the Federation’s daily operations. The administration will be headed by Secretary General Alina Dvoretskaya. Her team will execute FIDE’s decisions and coordinate the ongoing work of the various departments. The first stage covers four key areas. Marat Umutpayev – Legal Marat Umutpayev is an international lawyer from Kazakhstan who has worked on cross-border legal matters. At FIDE, he will provide legal support for the Federation’s activities and ensure compliance with its regulations. Nadezhda Kravchuk – External Relations & Communications Nadezhda Kravchuk has held several roles within FIDE, taking increasing responsibility over time. She now moves to a position covering external relations and communications. Her path within the Federation illustrates the opportunities for professional growth that the new structure aims to encourage. Anton Zhuravlev – Events Anton Zhuravlev, who has spent many years organising major international chess competitions, will head the Events department. His duties will include planning events and coordinating with tournament organisers. Pavel Tregubov – Sports Grandmaster Pavel Tregubov, a former European Champion, has experience in international chess administration. In his new role, he will oversee sporting matters, including competition regulations and cooperation with the relevant FIDE bodies. The next stage FIDE is building a team that draws on the experience of its current staff and the expertise of professionals joining the organisation. The new structure offers opportunities for internal career development and creates room for new people to contribute to the Federation’s work. The process of forming the administrative team is ongoing. FIDE welcomes expressions of interest from qualified professionals who would like to join the organisation and take on other roles within its administration. A detailed overview of the departments and their areas of responsibility is outlined in the new organisational structure. Further announcements regarding the administrative team will follow in due course.

title: Fujairah to host WFCC Grand Prix Final: World’s best solvers and composers to compete for €30,000
summary: The World Federation for Chess Composition (WFCC) is pleased to announce that the Grand Final of the WFCC Fujairah Grand Prix 2025–2026 will take place from 27 to 30 November 2026 in Fujairah, United Arab Emirates. The world’s leading chess solvers will meet in the new building of the Fujairah Chess & Culture Club, home of the WFCC Main Office, to decide the first Grand Prix champion, and to vote for the best of the original compositions created to challenge them. The new building of the Fujairah Chess & Culture Club, venue of the Grand Prix Final The event is held under the patronage of H.H. Sheikh Mohammed bin Hamad Al Sharqi, Crown Prince of Fujairah, on whose personal initiative the series was created. The project was realised by WFCC 1st Vice-President Abdulla Ali Aal Barket and WFCC Secretary Mohammad Alhallak, and the 2025–26 edition is the first cycle of what is planned to become a traditional competition. The road to Fujairah Qualification spanned four official championships: the European Chess Solving Championships in Athens (April 2025) and Skopje (May 2026), and the World Chess Solving Championships in Alba Iulia (July 2025) and Magdeburg (August 2026). Each solver’s two best results counted towards the overall standings. Piotr Murdzia (Poland) and Danila Pavlov (FIDE) finished the cycle tied at the top with 87 points each, ahead of Kacper Piorun (Poland) and Arno Zude (Germany), who both scored 72. Top-finishers of the World Chess Solving Championship 2026 in Magdeburg, from left: Piotr Murdzia (2nd), Danila Pavlov (1st) and Arno Zude (3rd) The finalists Following several withdrawals, the line-up of the final is as follows: From the top 12 of the Grand Prix standings: Piotr Murdzia (POL), Danila Pavlov (FIDE), Kacper Piorun (POL), Arno Zude (GER), Ural Khasanov (FID), Eddy Van Beers (BEL), Mihnea Costachi (ROU), Bilguun Sumiya (MGL), Maksim Kharitonov (FID), Nikos Sidiropoulos (GRE), and Kevinas Kuznecovas (LTU), who, in line with the regulations, replaces his compatriot Martynas Limontas from the reserve list Best solvers from other countries: Ilija Serafimović (SRB), Oleksiy Solovchuk (UKR), Joost Michielsen (NED) Organisers’ nominees: Anirudh Daga (IND), the best Indian junior solver, and Renars Muzis (LVA), winner of the Youth Chess Composing Challenge 2026 Still to be confirmed: solvers from the host Fujairah Chess & Culture Club and FIDE nominees Format and rating The Final consists of six rounds over two days in the familiar WCSC/ECSC format. On 28 November (11:00–14:30) solvers face two-movers, three-movers and endgame studies; on 29 November (10:00–13:30) helpmates, more-movers and self-mates. All 18 problems are original, previously unpublished compositions by 18 different composers. The tournament is rated with coefficient 3, and solving title norms can be achieved. As an invitational event, it does not form part of the World Solving Cup. A substantial prize fund With a total of €30,000, the Final offers a generous prize fund for a single chess-solving event. The solvers’ share of €27,000 is more than double the €12,000 awarded at each World Chess Solving Championship leg of the series, and the Final alone accounts for well over a third of the €74,000 distributed across the entire Grand Prix cycle. The winner will receive €3,800, with €2,900 for second and €2,400 for third place. Every finalist receives a prize of at least €750. All finalists are accommodated in single rooms on a full-board basis at the official hotel, Royal M Hotel by Gewan Fujairah. Composers and solvers: a duel and a dialogue Without composers there would be no solving competitions, and the Grand Final puts this relationship at its heart. All 18 problems and studies come from an accompanying composing tournament, in which problemists from around the world compete to create works that are beautiful, yet hard enough to challenge the best solvers in the world. At the end, the roles are reversed: for the first time, the solvers will reward the composers by vote. The finalists will rank the three compositions of each round for clarity, beauty, surprise and difficulty, and based on the marks of the top 10 solvers, the best composition in each round earns €500 – €3,000 in total. Preference is given to composers from countries not represented in the Final, and the selected works and their authors will be revealed on 29 November. The aim, as the composing tournament announcement puts it, is to “revive the dialogue between composers and solvers” – bringing together the two sides of chess composition. As previously announced on the official WFCC Fujairah Grand Prix website, the deadline for submissions is 1 November 2026. Entries (up to three per author) should be sent to Grand Prix Final Director Axel Steinbrink at axel.steinbrink@gmx.de. The dialogue will continue off the clock. On the evening of 28 November, a Youth Evening will see the five junior finalists – Renars Muzis, Ural Khasanov, Ilija Serafimović, Kevinas Kuznecovas and Anirudh Daga – present their own original compositions for the senior participants to solve. Afterwards the tables turn, as experienced finalists such as Piotr Murdzia and Joost Michielsen set their own problems for the juniors. Schedule Participants arrive on 27 November. The evening of 28 November, after the first competition day, is reserved for the Youth Evening. The closing ceremony takes place on 29 November at 19:00, followed by departures on 30 November. A separate blitz solving event for domestic solvers is planned for 29 November, with details to be announced. Full regulations, standings, and the list of finalists are available on the official website: https://grandprix.wfcc.ch/ Officials Tournament Director: Dr. Abdulla Ali Aal Barket Head of Technical Committee: GM Marjan Kovačević Head of Organising Committee: IA/IO Mohammad Alhallak Chief Arbiter: ISJ Axel Steinbrink Contact: grandprix@wfcc.ch   Written by: Dragana Nikolovska

title: A chess revival at Simpson's-in-the-Strand
summary:
The London chess café Simpson's-in-the-Strand was, for a time, a meeting place for the world's leading players. Now, thanks to Jeremy King and Jason Kouchak, the historic venue is enjoying a revival not only as a top restaurant but also as a gathering place for chess enthusiasts. | Photos: Chiao Lee

Simpson's-in-the-Strand in London is one of Europe's most famous chess cafés and was also a very exclusive restaurant where London high society regularly gathered for meals, conversation and, for many years, chess as well.

The establishment opened in 1828 under the name "Grand Cigar Divan". In the middle of the 19 th century, it was the meeting place of the English chess scene for more than 20 years. Anyone who wanted to see the world's best players at close quarters – Henry Bird, Wilhelm Steinitz or his rival for the claim of being the world's best player, Johannes Hermann Zukertort – or perhaps even play against them for money, had come to the right place.

It was here, at Simpson's, on the fringes of the first major international chess tournament of 1851, which marked the beginning of modern tournament chess, that the famous "Immortal Game" between Adolf Anderssen and Lionel Kieseritzky was played as a casual game.

In later years, chess players gradually receded into the background, and players found other meeting places or founded chess clubs. Even so, the chess tradition at Simpson's was maintained for a long time.

One of Simpson's regular visitors towards the end of the 19 th century was Arthur Conan Doyle (1859–1930), who would think about his detective stories while dining there. The restaurant is occasionally mentioned in his Sherlock Holmes novels.

Conan Doyle also had a connection with chess. His remark about the investigative method of his detective Sherlock Holmes can also be applied to calculation in chess.

"How often have I said to you that when you have eliminated the impossible, whatever remains, however improbable, must be the truth?"

Arthur Conan Doyle

At the beginning of the 20 th century, Simpson's was remodelled and for a time was regarded as the best restaurant in England. Chess, however, had long since ceased to be played there. After the 1980s, English chess enthusiasts tried to revive the tradition and organised a number of chess tournaments there. The establishment changed ownership several times at the beginning of the 21 st century and then stood empty for a while.

Eventually, Simpson’s-in-the-Strand was bought by the Savoy Hotel Group and reopened as a restaurant under the direction of restaurateur Jeremy King. But the chess tradition was also to be revived after the reopening.

Jeremy King appointed his friend, the musician and composer Jason Kouchak, as impresario for music and chess.

Last March, Simpson's hosted its first blindfold simultaneous exhibition in 100 years. Since the days of Philidor, blindfold play had been one of the special feats of the old masters, who played and won against one or even several opponents without looking at the board. English grandmaster Luke McShane revived that old blindfold tradition.

Recently, Jason Kouchak, together with Luke McShane and Stuart Conquest, organised another chess event at the legendary Simpson's. On 18 October, Luke McShane gave a blindfold simultaneous exhibition against three opponents. His opponents were fairly strong club players with ratings between 1850 and 2100.

Luke McShane

At the same time, Stuart Conquest played 12 opponents with sight of the boards in a "normal" simultaneous exhibition.

Jason Kouchak carries out Luke McShane's moves

Stuart Conquest begins his simultaneous exhibition

As a "Renaissance man", Jason Kouchak hosted the evening with flair and energy, complementing the historic setting with a suitably styled frock coat reminiscent of fashion from Philidor's era.

Jason Kouchak: Looking for inspiration

After the chess exhibition, his music was played during the jazz part of the evening.

After 40 minutes, Luke McShane had defeated all his opponents. The grandmaster gave an understandable reason for his superiority: "When I play blindfold, I have an advantage over my opponents. I am not distracted by the beautiful surroundings here."

The Final Movement: Jazz Chess!

One of Stuart Conquest's simultaneous opponents was Henry McWatters, chairman of the chess circle at the Royal Automobile Club. With a little luck, he managed to win his game. He has kindly made the wild and complicated encounter available here.

"Jeremy King is the white knight who saved the 'Home of Chess' - Simpson's in the Strand - and restored it to its former glory", Jason Kouchak said, delighted with the successful evening.

The well-known nature photographer Chiao Lee captured the "wild" moves on the chessboard and the "survival instincts of the knights in their struggle against the intuition and acuity of the grandmasters" (Jason Kouchak).

On 6 December, further surprise guests from the grandmaster community will be there to entertain, inspire and perhaps even surprise an enthusiastic chess audience.

With many thanks to Jason Kouchak for the inspiration and information.

title: Lhamsuren Myagmarsuren (1938-2026)
summary:
Bobby Fischer fans in particular will probably be familiar with the name Lhamsuren Myagmarsuren. At the Interzonal Tournament in Sousse 1967, Fischer defeated him in a brilliant game that is still frequently cited. On 26 October, the multiple Mongolian champion, who represented his country on numerous occasions, died at the age of 88. | Foto: https://montsame.mn/

Lhamsuren Myagmarsuren was born in 1938 in Buyant Sum district, in Chovd Province (Chovd Aimag), in western Mongolia. After finishing school, he studied geology at the Polytechnic Institute of the State University of Mongolia. He initially worked at the State Geological Fund of the Ministry of Science and Technology, and later at the Central Geological Administration of Mongolia, the International Geological Expedition and Mogoy Gol Gold "EBE" JSC. Over the course of his career, Myagmarsuren became one of Mongolia's leading geologists. Myagmarsuren compiled extensive maps, catalogues and databases documenting Mongolia's mineral resources, fossil sites in his home country and water resources in various regions. Until 2003, Myagmarsuren was the chief engineer at the Mogoy Gol gold mine in Yeroo.

In recognition of his achievements as a geologist, the Mongolian government named Myagmarsuren "Chief Geologist of Mongolia". He also received numerous other awards and decorations.

Alongside his successful career as a geologist, Myagmarsuren was also one of his country's best chess players for decades. He won the national championship four times (in 1965 and three consecutive years, 1980, 1981 and 1982). Between 1960 and 1982, he represented Mongolia at several World Student Team Championships and ten Chess Olympiads.

At the 1960 Chess Olympiad in Leipzig, Myagmarsuren was the best player on board four (16.5 points, best performance) and won the individual gold medal.

In addition to his appearances at the World Student Team Championships, Chess Olympiads and several military championships, Myagmarsuren rarely competed in international individual tournaments. However, by winning the West Asian Zonal Tournament in 1966, he qualified for the 1967 Interzonal Tournament in Sousse, where he faced players from the very top of the world elite. He often had to acknowledge the superiority of the professionals, as in his famous game against Bobby Fischer.

As is well known, Bobby Fischer, angered by several organisational shortcomings, withdrew from the tournament prematurely and needed a third attempt in 1970–72 before finally becoming world champion.

Occasionally, however, Myagmarsuren also managed to defeat opponents who were stronger on paper.

Perhaps his best game was played against Bent Larsen at the 1970 Chess Olympiad in Siegen.

In 1967, FIDE awarded him the title of International Master.

In 2004, Myagmasuren still took part in the World Senior Championships, and in 2009 he competed in a tournament in Ulaanbaatar. After that, however, he is said to have continued playing blitz games regularly on the ICC online platform under the name "Shatar".

For his achievements in chess, Myagmarsuren received the title of "Honoured Master of Sports" in 1996. In 1999, on the occasion of FIDE's 75th anniversary, his name was entered in the "Golden Book of World Chess". In 2020, he received a FIDE stipend in recognition of his achievements as a player.

Lhamsuren Myagmarsuren died on 26 October 2026. He was 88 years old.
